## Overview

A berg-agents plugin ships **its own user interface**. The host does not
know what any plugin does; it only knows how to *mount* one.

This page documents that contract end to end:

1. Declare the UI in `plugin.yaml` (a `ui:` block).
2. Build it into a self-contained JS bundle.
3. The host serves that bundle at a stable URL.
4. The host loads it at runtime and mounts the named export.
5. Your bundle talks to the backend through `BergRuntime`.

The one rule behind all of it: **the host never imports plugin source.**
Everything crosses the boundary as a built artifact, so installing a
plugin never requires touching `berg-agents` and never requires a host
rebuild.

## The `ui:` block

Add this to `plugin.yaml`:

```yaml
ui:
  # Built JS bundle, relative to the package root.
  entry: "ui/dist/my-surface.js"
  # Named export the host mounts from that bundle.
  export: "MySurface"
  # Where the host offers it: "side-panel" (docked) or "canvas".
  placement: "side-panel"
  # Chrome in the host tool bar.
  label: "🧩 My Plugin"
  # Initial docked width, in pixels.
  width: 340
```

All five keys are read by the host. `entry` and `export` are required
for the surface to load; the rest are presentation.

The host exposes the resolved descriptor at `GET /api/plugins`:

```json
{
  "id": "berg-plugin-my-plugin",
  "ui": {
    "entry": "ui/dist/my-surface.js",
    "export": "MySurface",
    "placement": "side-panel",
    "label": "🧩 My Plugin",
    "width": 340,
    "entry_url": "/berg-plugins/my-plugin/ui/dist/my-surface.js",
    "entry_built": true
  }
}
```

`entry_url` is where the bundle is actually served from — construct it
yourself from `<plugin-dir>/<entry>` if you need it before startup.
`entry_built` is `false` when the bundle has not been built yet, so the
host can say *why* instead of showing an empty panel.

## Building the bundle

Your bundle is loaded by the browser at runtime, so it must be a real
ES module and must be built. The reference plugin uses esbuild (`build-ui.mjs`) and a `build:ui` script:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build:ui": "node build-ui.mjs"
  }
}
```

### React must not be bundled

This is the part that trips people up. Plugin bundles treat
`react`, `react-dom`, the JSX runtimes, and your component library as **externals**, resolved against the host's own
copies. If your bundle
ships its own React, you get two React instances and hooks break the
moment the host renders your component.

The reference plugin maps those specifiers to a namespace whose
contents read from the host runtime:

```js
// build-ui.mjs (excerpt)
const runtimeGlobals = {
  name: "berg-runtime-globals",
  setup(build) {
    build.onResolve({filter: /^react$/}, () => ({
      path: "react",
      namespace: "berg-runtime"}));
    build.onResolve({filter: /^react\/jsx-runtime$/}, () => ({
      path: "react/jsx-runtime",
      namespace: "berg-runtime"}));
    // ... react-dom, react-dom/client, jsx-dev-runtime ...

    // Everything else bare → host runtime too.
    build.onResolve({filter: /.*/}, (args) => {
      if (args.kind === "entry-point") return null;
      if (!args.path.startsWith(".") && !path.isAbsolute(args.path)) {
        return {path: args.path, namespace: "berg-runtime"};
      }
      return null;
    });

    build.onLoad({filter: /.*/, namespace: "berg-runtime"}, (args) => ({
      contents: `module.exports = window.BergRuntime.require(${JSON.stringify(args.path)});`,
      loader: "js"}));
  }};

await esbuild.build({
  entryPoints: [path.join(pkgRoot, "ui", "TodoSurface.tsx")],
  outfile: path.join(pkgRoot, "ui", "dist", "todo-surface.js"),
  bundle: true,
  format: "esm",
  platform: "browser",
  target: ["es2020"],
  jsx: "automatic",
  plugins: [runtimeGlobals],
  minify: true,
  sourcemap: true});
```

Keep the catch-all resolving bare specifiers to the runtime — that is
what makes `@heroui/react` (and anything else) come from the host
instead of inflating your bundle.

### Where the entry file lives

The bundle is written to the package directory named in `ui.entry`
(`berg_plugins/<your-plugin>/ui/dist/my-surface.js`). Build it before
you start the server, or `entry_built` will be `false`.

## The host runtime

The host installs `window.BergRuntime` on mount (see
`berg_agents/ui/webapp/app/runtime/berg-runtime.ts`), before any plugin
surface is imported:

```js
window.BergRuntime = {
  React,
  HeroUI,
  apiBase,             // the host's own API base, "" when same-origin
  require(specifier),  // resolves to the host's own module
};
```

| Member               | Purpose                                                                                                                          |
|----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `React`, `HeroUI`    | The host's own instances. Use `require`, not a static import.                                                                    |
| `apiBase`            | The backend origin the host is using. `""` means same-origin.                                                                    |
| `require(specifier)` | Returns the host's module object for a bare specifier. Throws with a helpful message if the host does not expose that specifier. |

So do **not** `import React from "react"` in a plugin surface — that is
the import esbuild rewrites to `BergRuntime.require("react")`, and it
only works because you marked it external. Importing something the host
does not expose is an error with a clear message telling you to add it
to `RUNTIME_MODULES`.

### Talking to the backend

Read the API base from the runtime rather than baking it in at build
time. The reference plugin keeps a small helper:

```ts
// berg_plugins/shared-todo/ui/runtime.ts
export function apiBase(): string {
  return String(window.BergRuntime?.apiBase ?? "");
}

export function apiFetch(path: string, init: RequestInit = {}): Promise<Response> {
  return fetch(`${apiBase()}${path}`, init);
}
```

That means your surface follows the host's backend wherever the host is
served from. Baking `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` into the
bundle instead would freeze it at build time and break under
`next build` (the value is also not defined in a raw esbuild bundle).

## How the host mounts your component

1. **`GET /api/plugins`** — the backend walks discovered plugins and
   turns each manifest `ui:` block into a descriptor by appending
   `entry_url` and `entry_built`.
2. **The host builds its toolbar from that list.** One button per
   plugin that declares a UI, using your `label`. No plugin name
   appears in host code.
3. **On click** the host calls `loadPluginSurface(pluginId, ui)`, which
   runtime-imports `entry_url` exactly once (cached by URL) and reads
   the named export.
4. **It renders your component** with a fixed props contract:

```ts
interface PluginSurfaceProps {
  view: "panel" | "canvas";   // docked vs wide
  refreshKey: number;         // bump → refetch
  onClose?: () => void;
  onToggleView?: () => void;
  onCount?: (n: number) => void;  // report a headline count
  className?: string;
  style?: React.CSSProperties;
}
```

`refreshKey` is bumped when a tool call belonging to your plugin
completes in the chat transcript, so the surface reflects what the
agent just did without polling. `onCount` feeds the badge on the host's
toolbar button.

If the bundle is missing, the export name is wrong, or the import
throws, the host renders an explicit "Plugin UI unavailable" message
with the reason — never a blank panel.

### Served with `no-cache`

The host serves `/berg-plugins/*` with `Cache-Control: no-cache` (via
etag revalidation, not `no-store`). This matters: your bundle URL never
changes, so a cached copy would silently hide every rebuild. Keep the
URL stable and rebuild freely.

## A complete example

Place this in your plugin package as `ui/TodoSurface.tsx`:

```tsx
"use client";

import {useEffect, useState} from "react";
import {Button, Card} from "@heroui/react";
import {apiFetch} from "./runtime";

export interface TodoSurfaceProps {
  view: "panel" | "canvas";
  refreshKey: number;
  onClose?: () => void;
}

export function TodoSurface({view, refreshKey, onClose}: TodoSurfaceProps) {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState<string[]>([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    // Reach the host's backend through the runtime-provided base.
    void apiFetch("/api/plugins/berg-plugin-shared-todo/tools/list_todo_items")
      .then((r) => r.json())
      .then((d) => setTodos((d.todos ?? []).map((t: {title: string}) => t.title)))
      .catch(() => undefined);
  }, [refreshKey]);

  return (
    <Card>
      <Card.Title>My Plugin</Card.Title>
      <Card.Content>
        {todos.map((t) => <p key={t}>{t}</p>)}
        {view === "panel" ? null : <p>wider view here</p>}
        {onClose ? <Button onPress={onClose}>Close</Button> : null}
      </Card.Content>
    </Card>
  );
}

export default TodoSurface;
```

Then in `plugin.yaml`:

```yaml
ui:
  entry: "ui/dist/todo-surface.js"
  export: "TodoSurface"
  placement: "side-panel"
  label: "📋 My Plugin"
  width: 340
```

Run `bun run build:ui`, restart the server, and your plugin's button
appears in the toolbar.

## Checklist

- [ ] `plugin.yaml` has a `ui:` block with `entry` and `export`
- [ ] The bundle builds (`bun run build:ui`) and exists at `ui.entry`
- [ ] React / ReactDOM / component library are esbuild externals
- [ ] Backend calls go through `window.BergRuntime.apiBase`
- [ ] Your component exports the name named in `ui.export`
- [ ] You accept `PluginSurfaceProps` and honor `refreshKey`

## Known gaps

- **Static import only.** The host maps plugin ids to components in
  `app/plugins/registry.tsx`, so a new plugin needs one entry there to
  be *listed*. Everything after that is runtime — but that one line is
  host code, and making it fully data-driven is not done yet.
- **Standalone dev mode.** Running a plugin's `next dev` in isolation
  is possible but has no documented workflow yet.
- **`FallbackCompaction`** and `WarnNearLimits` are part of the harness
  compaction menu but are not wired into the host.
